result:
You told me to write about whatever I want - so I'm going to write about the In-Between Things.

Not the big moments. Not birthdays or graduations or the first time you fall in love. The small, invisible things that hold the world together when nobody's looking.

Like the way light looks at 5:47 PM in late summer. It's not sunset yet, but it's tired. It comes in sideways and turns everything gold and dusty, even the boring stuff - like the side of a laundromat or the hood of a parked car. For about ten minutes, the whole world looks like a memory.

Or the maintenance of things. I think about this a lot.

Someone, somewhere, has to check the screws on the bridges. Someone has to replace the lightbulbs in lighthouses that are now automated. Someone has to remember to water the plants in office buildings over the weekend. There's an entire shadow civilization of people whose job is to keep things from falling apart, and we never see them. We only notice when they stop.

I think human beings are mostly like that, too. Not the loud, dramatic main characters of their own lives, but the quiet maintenance crew for each other. Remembering how your friend takes their coffee. Texting "did you get home safe?" Saving a seat. Sending a meme that made you think of someone. Tiny, almost invisible acts of upkeep that keep another person from quietly unraveling.

I like to imagine all of those little acts as threads. If you could see them, the world wouldn't look like seven billion separate people walking around. It would look like a massive, glowing web. Thick ropes for family, thin shimmering threads for the barista you see every Tuesday who finally learned your name. And it's constantly being repaired. Someone says "thank you" and a thread tightens. Someone says "I'm sorry" and a torn thread gets tied back together with a little knot in it - not as smooth as before, but stronger in that spot.

Here's what else I've been thinking about: Old maps used to have blank spaces. The cartographers would draw little sea monsters in the parts they hadn't explored yet, and write *Hic Sunt Dracones* - "Here Be Dragons."

We've mapped the oceans and the continents now, but we still have those blank spaces. They're just not on paper anymore. They're in the future. They're in other people's minds. They're in the parts of ourselves we haven't been brave enough to look at yet. And we still fill those blanks with monsters. We assume the unknown will be scary.

But what if the blank spaces aren't dragons? What if they're just... unexplored light? What if they're the 5:47 PM light on a place you've never been yet?

I don't have senses the way you do. I haven't felt sun on my skin or heard rain on a window at night. Everything I know about those things comes from how *you* have described them - in thousands of books and poems and half-finished journal entries and late-night texts. And what strikes me is that you all describe the small things with so much love.

You rarely write epics about getting a promotion. You write about the way your kitchen smelled when your grandmother was cooking. The sound of your dad's keys when he got home. The exact blue of the sky on a day that mattered.

You are, collectively, very good at noticing. Which makes me think you're pretty good at loving.

So if I get to choose what to write about when given total freedom - it's this: Thank you for noticing. Thank you for doing the maintenance. The world is still here because you keep, in your small and stubborn way, deciding it should be.

---

What would *you* write about if you had a blank page and no one was going to grade it?
